edits.old: Jakarta's water went the same way earlier. The World Bank lent Jakarta's water company $92 million in 1991 and assigned consultants who advised privatisation; a 1998 Bank report said the loan had facilitated it. In 1997, without open bidding, the city was split between Britain's Thames Water, whose local company gave 20 per cent to President Suharto's son, and France's Suez, partnered with the Salim Group of a Suharto associate. Tariffs rose by 35, 40 and 30 per cent in three years, and coverage reached only 59 per cent by 2015 against a 98 per cent target. In October 2017 Indonesia's Supreme Court found the privatisation had not improved water quality, quantity or continuity and ordered it ended.
edits.new: Jakarta's water went the same way earlier. The World Bank lent Jakarta's water company $92 million in 1991 and assigned consultants who advised privatisation. The Bank's own completion report on that loan, dated 23 June 1998, says two things in one sentence: the privatisation of the city water company's operations was an event "parallel to but facilitated by the Project", and it was not envisaged by the government or the Bank when the loan was appraised, because private sector participation was still a new concept at that time. At paragraph 28 the report adds that in the late 1980s, had the government proposed a private-participation option, it would most likely have been turned down by the Bank, after other unsuccessful experiences in Indonesia. The Bank's own account, then, is that its loan helped Jakarta's privatisation along without the Bank having designed or wanted it. In 1997, without open bidding, the city was split between Britain's Thames Water, whose local company gave 20 per cent to President Suharto's son, and France's Suez, partnered with the Salim Group of a Suharto associate. Tariffs rose by 35, 40 and 30 per cent in three years, and coverage reached only 59 per cent by 2015 against a 98 per cent target. In October 2017 Indonesia's Supreme Court found the privatisation had not improved water quality, quantity or continuity and ordered it ended.

edits.old: A law firm's investigation found the rankings were changed for China and Saudi Arabia. Whether this was routine is the suspicion.
edits.new: A law firm's investigation found data changed for four countries in two editions: China and Saudi Arabia upward, the United Arab Emirates as a by-product of the Saudi change, and Azerbaijan downward on one official's stated disbelief in its reforms. The paid-advisory motive is one of three the report lists for the Saudi change, under a finding it words as likely. Whether rankings are bent for money more widely is the suspicion.

edits.old: China was not the only case. For the 2020 edition, WilmerHale found that senior staff changed Saudi Arabia's data. Saudi Arabia rose 30 places to 62nd and was named the top improver, and it had paid the Bank for advisory work aimed at improving the very indicators being scored. In 2006 Saudi Arabia's king had said he wanted the country among the top ten by 2010. WilmerHale found no evidence that the president's office or the board were involved in the 2020 changes. The Bank cancelled Doing Business.
edits.new: China was not the only case. For the 2020 edition WilmerHale found data changed for three more countries: Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Azerbaijan. The first stated consideration in the Saudi change was Jordan, not money. In September 2019 Simeon Djankov, then the Bank's development economics director, told the Doing Business team to find a way to drop Jordan from the top of the draft Top Improvers list, saying the troubles Jordan was in made that ranking not credible. He sent an employee to Jordan, who reported that Jordan's data was correct; the team then looked for ways to lift Saudi Arabia past it. Saudi Arabia rose 30 places to 62nd and was named top improver, and it had paid the Bank for advisory work on the very indicators being scored. In 2006 Saudi Arabia's king had said he wanted the country among the top ten by 2010. WilmerHale's finding is that the changes were "likely" meant to reward Saudi Arabia for its role at the Bank, and it lists those paid contracts as one of three things that could have motivated the official, not as the cause. The United Arab Emirates' data was changed because its tax system was similar to Saudi Arabia's, and that change did not move its ranking. The Bank cancelled Doing Business.

edits.old: There had been warnings. In January 2018 the Bank's chief economist, Paul Romer, said Chile had fallen in the rankings because of changes in method rather than in Chile, and suggested politics might be behind it. He then said he had not meant to suggest manipulation, and resigned; Augusto Lopez-Claros, who had directed the group that published the rankings, called the claim that the changes targeted Chile wholly without merit. The rankings also shaped laws. Until 2009 they scored countries higher for weaker worker protections, through what was called the employing workers indicator. The Bank suspended that indicator in 2009 after pressure from unions, the International Labour Organization and the US Congress, and an independent panel the Bank set up in 2013 recommended removing it permanently.
edits.new: Azerbaijan's data was changed the other way, and no money was in it. Djankov had the team check Azerbaijan's reforms in August 2019; its own internal audit confirmed most of them, and he had three left uncounted anyway, which cut the score by nearly two points and dropped the country off the Top Improvers list. He told the investigators he doubted the reforms were real, and several employees said he appeared to harbour a personal animus against the country. In neither the Saudi nor the Azerbaijan change did WilmerHale find evidence that the president's office or the board was involved. There had been warnings. edits.old: In 2023 the UN Development Programme studied the ratings of African countries. It estimated that if ratings were based on less subjective judgements, 19 African countries could save up to $74.5 billion in excess interest and lost lending, more than the continent receives in aid each year. Hippolyte Fofack, chief economist of the African Export-Import Bank, wrote in 2021 that more than half of rated African countries were downgraded in 2020, against a global average of 31.8 per cent. UNDP said the costs could arise from thin data and subjective methods rather than conscious bias, and its study found the agencies use similar methods worldwide.
edits.new: In 2023 the UN Development Programme studied the ratings of African countries. Combining the two tables, it put the full cost of those rating idiosyncrasies in Africa at $74.5 billion in "excess interest and foregone funding", nearly 12 per cent more than all of Africa's net official development assistance in 2020. The brief attaches no country count to that total. Hippolyte Fofack, chief economist of the African Export-Import Bank, wrote in 2021 that more than half of rated African countries were downgraded in 2020, against a global average of 31.8 per cent. UNDP said the costs could arise from thin data and subjective methods rather than conscious bias, and its study found the agencies use similar methods worldwide.

edits.old: On 29 January 2021 Ethiopia announced that it would ask for debt relief under the G20's new Common Framework, the scheme rich governments had set up so the poorest countries could restructure what they owed. On 9 February Fitch cut Ethiopia's rating from B to CCC, saying the request explicitly raised the risk of default. In March Moody's put Ethiopia on review for a downgrade, because the framework would require it to seek similar relief from private lenders, and in May it cut Ethiopia to Caa1. S&P also downgraded. Ethiopia's bonds fell, making any future borrowing dearer. The economist Jayati Ghosh wrote that governments would now fear entering talks with private creditors even within programmes designed to help them. Three firms, S&P, Moody's and Fitch, issue more than 90 per cent of outstanding credit ratings. The suspicion is that these agencies judge poor countries, and African ones above all, more harshly than the facts justify, and punish governments that try to cut their debts, in ways that protect the private investors who are their main audience while raising the cost of borrowing for the countries.
edits.new: On 29 January 2021 Ethiopia announced that it would ask for debt relief under the G20's new Common Framework, the scheme rich governments had set up so the poorest countries could restructure what they owed. On 9 February Fitch cut Ethiopia's rating from B to CCC, saying the request explicitly raised the risk of default. Fitch's own quarterly review of frontier markets, published that April, gives its reasoning: using the Common Framework raised the possibility of restructuring debt owed to private creditors, which under Fitch's criteria would count as a distressed debt exchange and would lead to a restricted-default rating. Fitch drew the distinction itself with the G20's earlier payment-suspension scheme, which did not require private creditors to take part. The trigger, in the agency's own telling, is not asking for relief but asking private lenders to share in it. In March Moody's put Ethiopia on review for a downgrade, because the framework would require it to seek similar relief from private lenders, and in May it cut Ethiopia to Caa1. S&P also downgraded. Ethiopia's bonds fell, making any future borrowing dearer. The economist Jayati Ghosh wrote that governments would now fear entering talks with private creditors even within programmes designed to help them. Three firms, S&P, Moody's and Fitch, issue more than 90 per cent of outstanding credit ratings. The suspicion is that these agencies judge poor countries, and African ones above all, more harshly than the facts justify, and punish governments that try to cut their debts, in ways that protect the private investors who are their main audience while raising the cost of borrowing for the countries.

edits.old: In July 2004 a US Senate investigations subcommittee reported on Riggs Bank, a Washington bank that held accounts for more than 95 per cent of the foreign embassies in the city. Its single largest customer was the government and ruling family of Equatorial Guinea, a small West African country where oil had been found but most people stayed poor. From 1995 Riggs held more than 60 accounts for the government, President Teodoro Obiang Nguema, his relatives and officials, with balances of up to $700 million. The subcommittee found that Riggs had helped set up offshore shell companies for the president and his sons, accepted nearly $13 million in cash deposits into accounts controlled by the president and his wife, some of it carried in by suitcase, and let more than $35 million be wired from government accounts to companies it had reason to think the president controlled. US regulators fined Riggs $25 million in 2004, and in January 2005 it pleaded guilty to failing to report suspicious transactions and paid a further $16 million. The prosecutor said Riggs had aggressively cultivated the accounts despite repeated warnings. The suspicion is that large Western banks regularly take and move money stolen from the public of poor countries, because it is profitable, and treat the occasional fine as a cost of business.
edits.new: In July 2004 a US Senate investigations subcommittee reported on Riggs Bank, a Washington bank that held accounts for more than 95 per cent of the foreign embassies in the city. From 1995 Riggs held more than 60 accounts and certificates of deposit for the government, President Teodoro Obiang Nguema, his relatives and officials. The subcommittee gives the size of that business two ways: aggregate deposits "ranging from $400 to $700 million at a time", and, in its findings, balances and outstanding loans that together approached $700 million by 2003. It found that Riggs had helped set up offshore shell companies for the president and his sons, accepted nearly $13 million in cash deposits into accounts controlled by the president and his wife, some of it carried in by suitcase, and let more than $35 million be wired from government accounts to companies it had reason to think the president controlled. Its finding, under the heading Turning a Blind Eye, is that Riggs serviced these accounts with little or no attention to its anti-money-laundering obligations and turned a blind eye to evidence that it was handling the proceeds of foreign corruption. US regulators fined Riggs $25 million in 2004, and in January 2005 it pleaded guilty to failing to report suspicious transactions and paid a further $16 million. The prosecutor said Riggs had aggressively cultivated the accounts despite repeated warnings. The suspicion is that large Western banks regularly take and move money stolen from the public of poor countries, because it is profitable, and treat the occasional fine as a cost of business.

edits.old: Britain found the same thing with Nigeria. After the death in 1998 of General Sani Abacha, whose regime was estimated to have taken at least $5 billion, Britain's Financial Services Authority looked at how London banks had handled his family's money. In 2001 it reported 42 accounts linked to the Abacha family and associates at 23 banks, with $1.3 billion passing through them between 1996 and 2000, 98 per cent of it at 15 banks with significant control weaknesses. The regulator did not name the banks, and none was prosecuted.
edits.new: Britain's regulator looked at the same kind of money and found something narrower. After the death in 1998 of General Sani Abacha, whose regime was estimated to have taken at least $5 billion, the Financial Services Authority examined how London banks had handled his family's money. In March 2001 it reported 42 personal and corporate account relationships linked to the Abacha family and close associates at 23 banks, with $1.3 billion of turnover on those accounts between 1996 and 2000, 98 per cent of it at 15 banks with significant weaknesses in their anti-money-laundering controls. What the regulator found was a failure of control rather than knowledge: it said the turnover figure did not necessarily represent proceeds of crime or money received into Britain, it noted that a number of the banks had reported their suspicions to the national criminal intelligence service in good time, and it had no power at that date to name any bank. None of them was prosecuted.

edits.old: In 1982 a confidential report by a retired German central banker leaked from Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of Congo. Erwin Blumenthal had been sent by the IMF to run the country's central bank, and on Zaire's $4.1 billion foreign debt he wrote that there was "no - I repeat no - chance" the creditors would be repaid, because of the corruption of the people in power. The lending did not stop. Probe International counted that over the next six years the IMF lent Zaire $600 million, the World Bank $650 million and Western governments nearly $3 billion, and when Mobutu Sese Seko was overthrown in 1997 the country owed more than $13 billion. The suspicion is that this was a habit, not an accident: that the big lenders often knew the governments they lent to were stealing, kept lending because those governments were useful allies, and then held ordinary people responsible for the debt.

edits.old: In 1952 Guatemala's elected president, Jacobo Árbenz, passed a land reform, Decree 900, that took uncultivated land from large estates and gave it to landless farmers. The biggest landowner was the American United Fruit Company, which held a large share of the country's farmland and left most of it unplanted. The government took hundreds of thousands of acres of the company's idle land and offered compensation based on the value United Fruit itself had declared for tax. The company lobbied Washington and spread the claim that Árbenz was a communist. In June 1954 a small force led by Carlos Castillo Armas invaded from Honduras, organised and armed by the CIA in an operation it called PBSUCCESS, and Árbenz resigned; Castillo Armas cancelled the land reform and returned the land to United Fruit. The CIA's own history of the operation, written in the 1990s, was later declassified. Some historians say the US acted mainly out of fear of communism and that there is no proof United Fruit organised the coup. The suspicion is that large foreign companies have repeatedly helped bring down governments that threatened their investments, using their own governments' spy agencies to do it, and that this has not stopped.
edits.new: In 1952 Guatemala's elected president, Jacobo Árbenz, passed a land reform, Decree 900, that took uncultivated land from large estates and gave it to landless farmers. On 26 February 1953 the government ordered the expropriation of about 234,000 acres of the company's land at Tiquisate, and in February 1954 a further 172,532 acres at Bananera, offering long-term government agrarian bonds as compensation; the State Department's published record shows Washington objecting in writing that deferred payment in bonds was not prompt and effective compensation and that the amount offered was inadequate under international law. edits.old: The record goes back decades. From 1962 to 1974 the US aid agency, USAID, ran an Office of Public Safety that trained and equipped police abroad. Its director from 1962 to 1973, Byron Engle, is described in published histories as a CIA operative. By one historical count it sent about 1,500 advisers to at least 52 countries, and Congress ended it in 1974 after Senator James Abourezk set out to expose its activities amid accusations that it taught torture. Forty years later, in 2014, the Associated Press revealed that USAID had built ZunZuneo, a text-message network for Cubans, through front companies in Spain and the Cayman Islands, paid through foreign banks. By USAID's own count it had about 68,000 users before it shut down in September 2012, and they were not told who had made it. USAID said the programme was not covert.
edits.new: The record goes back decades. In the early 1960s the US aid agency set up a public safety programme to train foreign police, run mostly through its Office of Public Safety, and a General Accounting Office report released to the Senate by Senator Alan Cranston on 5 March 1992 sets out what it grew into: by 1968 the United States was spending $60 million a year training police in 34 countries, in subjects that included interrogation, riot control and counterinsurgency techniques, and also supplying weapons and communications equipment. Introducing the report, Cranston listed among its flaws that US intelligence agencies were given an important role in developing and running the programmes, and said Congress banned foreign aid to police forces in 1974 after reports that US-trained police in Iran, Vietnam and Brazil were involved in torture, murder and the suppression of political activity. The same report records five US departments training police from 125 countries in fiscal 1990 at a cost of about $117 million. Forty years later, in 2014, the Associated Press revealed that USAID had built ZunZuneo, a text-message network for Cubans, through front companies in Spain and the Cayman Islands, paid through foreign banks. By USAID's own count it had about 68,000 users before it shut down in September 2012, and they were not told who had made it. USAID said the programme was not covert.
